title: Effects of Strength Training on the Physiological Determinants of Middle- and Long-Distance Running Performance: A Systematic Review
authors: Blagrove RC, Howatson G, Hayes PR
population: Middle- and long-distance runners with at least 6 months of running experience; 24 controlled studies (heavy, explosive or plyometric training of 4 weeks or more versus a running-only control)
findings: 24 studies met the inclusion criteria; PEDro internal validity scores were 4, 5 or 6.
Running economy was measured in 20 studies and generally improved by 2-8% versus control, although not in every study.
Time trial performance (1.5-10 km) and anaerobic speed qualities also tended to improve.
VO2max, velocity at VO2max, blood lactate and body composition were typically unaffected; body composition was not negatively impacted.
Authors conclude that two to three strength sessions per week, including a variety of modalities, are likely to benefit middle- and long-distance runners.
limitations: Narrative synthesis with no pooled effect size; low PEDro scores (4-6); heterogeneous protocols; findings not consistent across all studies; no ultra-distance or masters focus. The 2-3 sessions per week statement is a recommendation, not a tested dose-response.
implications: Default to 2 strength sessions per week; allow 3 for athletes with a lifting background in base phases; do not exceed 3.
Mix modalities in a block (heavy resistance plus plyometric/explosive work) rather than a single method.
State the expected running economy gain as a modest range (about 2-8% in the literature, with a conservative planning figure lower) and do not promise a VO2max or threshold change.
Assume no body-mass penalty from lower-body strength work for distance runners.
